title: N-Ch-M

cards: A house with the mirrors covered. The front door is left unlocked so nobody has to ring. Inside, the mourners sit on low stools, and visitors come in quietly with trays of food and sit near them.
By an old custom, the visitors don't start talking. They wait, sometimes a long while, until the mourner speaks first.
Leaving, they say a set line in Hebrew, something like: may God, called here the Place, comfort you among the mourners of Zion and Jerusalem. The verb in that line, yenachem, comes from today's root.

teach.b: N-Ch-M. Nun, chet, mem. Nechamah, comfort.
Turn it four ways. First, the prophet. Isaiah chapter forty opens: "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God."
In Hebrew, nachamu, nachamu: said twice, as if once weren't enough.
That chapter is read on the Shabbat after Tisha b'Av, the day of mourning for the Temples, and that Shabbat takes its name from the first word: Shabbat Nachamu. Second, a baby's name.

teach.h: NOAH: THIS SAME SHALL COMFORT US.
teach.b: When Noah is born, his father Lamech explains the name: "This same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands."

The text ties the boy's name to comfort, after the curse on the ground that made work so hard. Third, Joseph. After Jacob dies, his brothers are afraid Joseph will finally pay them back for selling him.
Instead, "he comforted them, and spake kindly unto them."
More literally, he spoke to their heart: not a speech about what went wrong, but words aimed at the heart. Fourth, the shiva house, which you sat in earlier this year.

teach.h: YENACHEM: MAY THE PLACE COMFORT YOU.

teach.b: The visitors don't claim to do the comforting themselves. They sit, they wait, they bring food, and they hand the comfort back to the Place.
A prophet's doubled cry, a baby's name, a brother's kind words, a quiet visit: one root.

how: Visitors to a shiva house sit with the mourners, wait for them to speak first, and on leaving say ha-Makom yenachem, may the Place comfort you; the Shabbat after Tisha b'Av is called Shabbat Nachamu, after the opening of Isaiah 40, its prophetic reading.

o: comfort, the kind given to those who mourn
a feast held to celebrate a new baby's birth
advice that explains why a loss happened

s: Shabbat Nachamu takes its name from Isaiah's comfort ye
it's read on the Shabbat after Tisha b'Av.
Joseph's brothers got a lecture about what they had done
"he comforted them, and spake kindly unto them."
at a shiva, visitors are expected to start the conversation
by custom they wait for the mourner to speak first.

games.q: you walk into a shiva house. the mourner is sitting low and silent. what does custom ask of you first?
o: tell them it all happened for a reason.
sit near them and wait for them to speak.
talk about something cheerful to take their mind off it.
games.why: wait. the Talmud teaches that comforters don't speak until the mourner opens. the comfort itself is handed back to the Place: yenachem.

practice: Bring to mind one person carrying something heavy, a loss, an illness, a job gone, a quiet loneliness, and picture yourself sitting near them the way visitors sit at a shiva: not fixing, not explaining, just there.
Think of a few words aimed at the heart, the way Joseph spoke to his brothers, and hold them until they feel right; if you pray, you can ask that they be comforted.
And if the heavy thing is yours, and you're in danger or thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: N-Ch-M. Nun, chet, mem: nechamah, comfort, from nachamu to yenachem. This week's roots ran soul, earth, keep, work, king, redeem, and comfort. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: comfort ye, the opening of Isaiah 40, said twice.

carryVoice: Your line: comfort. Sometimes it's simply being there, with words aimed at the heart. Go gently.
